claims.text: In solidified FeNiCrMn, dynamic tensile strength and ductility are primarily governed by a temperature- and strain-rate-dependent switch between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
Lower temperatures and higher strain rates reduce thermal activation and increase the barrier for dislocation nucleation.
An increased barrier to dislocation nucleation favors deformation twinning as an alternative plasticity mechanism.
Higher temperatures lower the barrier to dislocation nucleation and make dislocation slip more favorable.
Lower strain rates favor dislocation slip over deformation twinning.
The density and arrangement of dynamically formed dislocations and twins depend on crystallographic orientation, temperature, and strain rate.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate tension will produce an enhanced twin population.
Enhanced twinning at low temperature and high strain rate will be accompanied by higher apparent yield stress and sustained ductility.
High-temperature, low-strain-rate tension will be dominated by dislocation activity.
Dislocation-dominated deformation at higher temperatures and lower strain rates will result in a lower yield point and increased ductility.
At room temperature and moderate strain rate along a principal crystallographic direction, FeNiCrMn initially exhibits mixed dislocation and limited twin activity.
The proposed scope is limited to idealized, defect-minimized solidified FeNiCrMn and excludes reliable treatment of precipitates, grain-boundary effects, and extrinsic defects.
The target alloy is Co-free equiatomic FeNiCrMn produced by fusion processing.

contradictions.description: The conditions permit idealized polycrystalline simulations, while the boundary says grain-boundary effects may not be accounted for. A polycrystalline model necessarily contains grain boundaries unless they are explicitly disabled or treated as outside the inference.
